extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties (petitioners/patent owners) in PTAB inter partes review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and applied criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board to decide whether to institute an inter partes review, including statutory thresholds, claim construction, obviousness analysis, and discretionary denial under parallel proceedings. The page is an institution decision applying these standards to claims of a particular patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable likelihood to institute (35 U.S.C. § 314(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a), the Board “may not authorize an inter partes review to be instituted unless . . . the information presented in the petition . . . and any response . . . shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the threshold for institution — the Board evaluates the petition, any preliminary response, and the evidence of record to determine whether petitioner has demonstrated a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one challenged claim. Findings made for institution are preliminary and not final; final determinations depend on the full trial record. By rule and SAS/ Iancu, when instituting review the Board must authorize review on all challenged claims and on all grounds asserted for each claim (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition particularity requirement (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3); 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: “The petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable.” (Harmonic Inc.). 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4) require the petition to identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds and to specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions must map claim elements to specific disclosures in cited references and explain how the references render the claims unpatentable. This burden never shifts to Patent Owner. Lack of particularity is a basis to deny institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standard for obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103; Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is resolved based on Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) secondary considerations (objective indicia). The Board applies these factual determinations when assessing whether a petitioner has shown a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on obviousness grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board preliminarily defines the level of skill in the art (POSITA) relevant to the challenged claims using evidence in the record (e.g., education, degrees, and practical experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The POSITA definition should be grounded in the patent and cited prior art and the parties’ evidence. The Board may adopt a preliminary definition (here: bachelor’s degree in electrical or mechanical engineering and two years' experience in designing/implementing hardware components) and notes that more experience can compensate for lack of a degree. Parties may suggest clarifications; the POSITA determination informs claim meaning and obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are construed according to Phillips v. AWH Corp.: terms receive their ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art, read in the context of the claim and the entire patent, including the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board construes terms as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) per 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b). Only those claim terms that are in controversy need be expressly construed and only to the extent necessary to resolve the dispute (Nidec/Vivid). Parties should point to specific portions of the specification, prosecution history, and relevant extrinsic evidence when arguing constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part Advanced Bionics framework for discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 325(d), the Director/Board may deny institution when the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments previously were presented to the Office. Advanced Bionics establishes a two-part test: (1) whether the same/substantially the same art or arguments were previously presented to the Office in proceedings pertaining to the challenged patent; and (2) if so, whether the petitioner has demonstrated that the Office erred in a manner material to the patentability of the challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings that count as previously presenting art include examination of the application, reexamination, reissue, and AIA post-grant proceedings. The Board weighs whether the parallel Office proceeding is more advanced and involves overlapping issues (see Notice Regarding Amendment Options). The second part requires a showing of material error by the Office in prior evaluation. Board precedents (Intromedic, Fox Factory, Mueller) and posture of the parallel proceeding (e.g., whether prosecution closed or claims amended, how long art has been under consideration) factor into whether to exercise discretion to deny.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as 'previously presented' art/arguments and when denial is appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Art/arguments must have been presented during proceedings pertaining to the challenged patent for § 325(d) to apply; merely being in an early-stage third-party filing is not always sufficient to deny institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board compares the stage and substance of the parallel proceeding: if the parallel proceeding is more advanced, has resulted in claim amendments or a completed reexamination considering the same art, denial under § 325(d) is more likely. If the parallel proceeding is in an early stage, or claims have not been amended and the Office has not made a final determination, the Board may decline to exercise discretion to deny. Prejudice (e.g., statutory bars to filing an IPR) also weighs against denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption regarding separately listed claim limitations and when they may be satisfied by the same prior-art structure (Becton Dickinson / Google clarification)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that separately listed claim limitations may indicate separate and distinct physical structure, but that presumption can be rebutted by the intrinsic record of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becton, Dickinson is not a per se rule; Google LLC v. EcoFactor clarified that the presumption is rebuttable. The Board examines the intrinsic record (specification, claim language) to determine whether a single structure in a prior reference can satisfy multiple claim limitations. Expert testimony and reference disclosures may support such a mapping where the patent does not demand separate physical structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of foreign-language references and translations (37 C.F.R. § 1.68 requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: English translations submitted for foreign-language references must be accompanied by affidavits complying with 37 C.F.R. § 1.68.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a submitted translation's affidavit does not meet regulatory requirements, the petitioner is required to re-submit the translation with a corrected affidavit. Noncompliant affidavits may be noted and corrected as a condition of institution or trial readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAS rule on institution scope (37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When instituting review, the Board will authorize the review to proceed on all of the challenged claims and on all grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board's institution decision is necessarily on all challenged claims and all grounds asserted in the petition; the Board will not partially institute on a subset of claims/grounds (SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary nature of institution findings and parties' opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's findings of fact and conclusions of law in an institution decision are not final and are made for the sole purpose of determining whether to institute review; final decisions are based on the full trial record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Owner is warned that arguments not raised in a timely-filed Response may be deemed forfeited even if presented in a Preliminary Response. The institution-stage analysis is limited to the record before the Board at institution and may be revisited during trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: How claim element mappings and obviousness combinations are evaluated at institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board examines whether the cited references teach the claim elements (including structural placements and functional interconnections) and whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine references with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board reviews the references, expert declarations, annotated figures, and arguments from parties. Disputes about whether a reference discloses a limitation (e.g., location of a socket or whether separate structures are required) are resolved preliminarily with attention to intrinsic record, prior-art disclosure, and expert testimony. Where reasonable factual disputes remain, the Board may still institute if petitioner shows a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one claim.
